1.exp: Book-keeping = keeping the record (recording) of transactions. A and B are later stages (analysis/audit); D has nothing to do with book-keeping.
1.concept: Book-keeping = recording; Accounting = recording + classifying + summarising + interpreting.

2.exp: Internal users are inside the business (Owner, Manager). Bank, Investor and Tax Dept are external users.

3.exp: Land and Building are assets used for a long time = Fixed Assets.
3.concept: Fixed asset = asset bought for long-term use (more than 1 year).

4.exp: A creditor is someone to whom we owe money (a supplier). A describes Debtors. In D cash is already received, so there is no payable/receivable.

5.exp: Money will be received from Debtors, so it is an Asset (Current Asset).

6.exp: Salary is a cost of running the business (Expense). Capital and Loan are sources of funds; Sale is Income.
6.concept: Expense = cost incurred to earn income.

7.exp: A = L + C. The other options have wrong signs/sides. E.g. by B, with Assets 1,20,000 and Liabilities 35,000 Capital would be 1,55,000, which is wrong.

8.exp: Transactions of the business and the owner are kept separate. Money the owner takes for personal use = Drawings. B is Going Concern; C and D are wrong.
8.concept: Entity concept: the business is treated as a separate person.

9.exp: Going Concern = the business will continue in the future. That is why fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation.

10.exp: Accrual: show an expense in the period it belongs to, not when it was paid. So March has Outstanding Rent.

11.exp: Only transactions that can be measured in money are recorded. Other qualities matter but cannot be measured in rupees.

12.exp: Drawings = money taken by the owner → Capital decreases, Cash (asset) decreases. The equation stays balanced.
12.concept: Drawings reduce capital; they are not an Expense.

13.exp: Capital = A − L = 2,50,000 − 80,000 = ₹1,70,000. A (3,30,000) is the sum — the wrong method.

14.exp: Assets = L + C = 1,20,000 + 3,00,000 = ₹4,20,000. A is a subtraction — wrong.

16.exp: Cash (asset) ↑ and Capital ↑ — both sides rise by ₹1,00,000.

17.exp: Stock ↑ (asset) and Creditors ↑ (liability). Capital does not change.

18.exp: Furniture ↑ and Cash ↓ — one asset swapped for another; total Assets stay the same. In A, B and C total Assets increase.
18.concept: Some transactions only convert one asset into another.

19.exp: Not yet paid but owed — so it is a Liability (Current Liability).
19.concept: Outstanding expense = Liability; Prepaid expense = Asset.

20.exp: Capital before = 5,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 3,00,000. After the loan A = 6,00,000, L = 3,00,000, so Capital is still ₹3,00,000. A loan is not capital.
20.concept: Taking a loan does not change Capital.

21.concept: Verify A = L + C after all transactions.

22.exp: Opening Capital = 4,00,000 − 1,50,000 = 2,50,000. Closing = 2,50,000 + 70,000 − 20,000 = ₹3,00,000. C did not deduct drawings; D wrongly added/subtracted the profit.

23.exp: Bank (asset) ↓ 40,000 and Creditors (liability) ↓ 40,000. Assets = 6,00,000 − 40,000 = ₹5,60,000; Liabilities 2,00,000 + Capital 3,60,000 = 5,60,000 ✓.
23.concept: Paying a liability reduces both Asset and Liability.

1.exp: Personal account (person/organisation): the one who receives is Debited, the one who gives is Credited. A is the Real account rule, C is the Nominal account rule; D is the reverse.
1.concept: Personal: Debit the receiver, Credit the giver.

2.exp: Ramesh is a person → Personal. Cash and Furniture = Real; Salary = Nominal.

3.exp: Real account (assets): what comes in is Debited, what goes out is Credited. E.g. cash received → Cash A/c Debit.
3.concept: Real: Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out.

5.exp: The owner's capital is like a liability (the business owes it to the owner) → Credit balance. Drawings, however, have a Debit balance.
5.concept: Capital = Credit balance; Drawings = Debit balance.

6.exp: Rent is an Expense (Nominal): Debit all expenses. Cash decreased, so Cash is Credited.

7.exp: Narration = the short explanation (Being …) written below the entry.

8.exp: L.F. = Ledger Folio (page/account number in the ledger).
8.concept: Journal columns: Date, Particulars, L.F., Dr, Cr.

9.exp: Purchases (expense/trading) is Debited; cash went out, so Cash is Credited. A is the reverse entry.
9.concept: Cash purchase: Purchases Dr, Cash Cr.

10.exp: Bank (comes in) Debit; Cash (goes out) Credit. A is the entry for withdrawing from the bank.
10.concept: Deposit into bank: Bank Dr, Cash Cr.

11.concept: Credit sale: Debtor Dr, Sales Cr.

12.exp: Cash came in → Debit; Mahesh's dues are cleared → Credit him. Sales are not recorded again (already recorded).
12.concept: Receipt from debtor: Cash Dr, Debtor Cr.

13.exp: Returning goods reduces what we owe Ram → Ram Debit; Purchases Return (a credit-balance account) Credit. D (Sales Return) is wrong.
13.concept: Purchase return: Supplier Dr, Purchases Return Cr.

14.exp: Debit: Cash 4,900 + Discount Allowed 100 (loss) = 5,000; Credit: Suresh 5,000. Dr total = Cr total ✓. C has the sides reversed; in D, Suresh's ₹100 stays unsettled.
14.concept: Discount allowed = expense (Debit); Discount received = income (Credit).

15.exp: Owner withdrew goods: Drawings Debit; Purchases (goods) Credit. Do not show it as a sale.

16.exp: The expense belongs to this year → Salary Debit; unpaid → Outstanding Salary (Liability) Credit. B credits cash although nothing was paid.
16.concept: Outstanding expense: Expense Dr, Outstanding A/c Cr.

17.exp: 1 Oct–31 Mar = 6 months used; 6 months remain. Prepaid = 12,000 × 6/12 = ₹6,000. D reflects 9 months — wrong.
17.concept: Prepaid expense = expense paid in advance for a future period (Asset).

18.exp: Installation is part of the machinery's cost (capital expenditure). Debit Machinery = 50,000 + 5,000 = ₹55,000; Credit Bank 50,000 + Cash 5,000.
18.concept: Cost of an asset = price + installation/freight.

19.exp: Purchases Dr 40,000; To Cash 25,000; To Rahul 15,000 (40,000 − 25,000). C wrongly treats the whole amount as credit.
19.concept: Compound entry: total Debit = total Credit.

21.exp: Bank is an Asset; money went out so it is Credited (Real account rule). Entry: Ram A/c Dr 6,000; To Bank A/c 6,000.

22.exp: Bad debt is an Expense/Loss → Debit; Kiran's receivable ends → Credit Kiran.
22.concept: Bad debts: Bad Debts Dr, Debtor Cr.

23.exp: Trade discount is not recorded separately; record at invoice value = 10,000 − 1,000 = ₹9,000. Purchases Dr 9,000; To Raj 9,000.
23.concept: Trade discount is not recorded; cash discount is.

24.exp: Cash Dr 3,000; To Commission Received (Nominal, Income) 3,000. Income = Credit.

1.exp: Entries in the Journal are posted account-wise into the ledger. So Ledger = principal book of accounts.
1.concept: Ledger = book of accounts; Journal → Ledger posting.

2.exp: The same side (Dr/Cr) as in the Journal. Debit → left side.
2.concept: The side does not change during posting.

3.exp: More cash cannot go out than you have, so the Cash A/c normally has a Debit balance (or nil). A Credit balance would mean negative cash — impossible.

4.exp: Cash transactions are recorded directly in the Cash Book (Journal function) and it also works as the Cash A/c ledger; so separate posting is not needed.
4.concept: Cash Book = subsidiary book + Cash Ledger.

5.exp: E.g. cash deposited in the bank: Bank Dr, Cash Cr — both in the Cash Book; "C" is written on both sides.

6.exp: A Trial Balance lists all ledger balances in Debit/Credit columns to check whether the totals agree.

7.exp: Purchases (Expense) = Debit balance. Capital, Sales (Income) and Creditors (Liability) = Credit balance.
7.concept: TB: Assets + Expenses = Debit; Liabilities + Capital + Income = Credit.

8.exp: Purchases Book = credit purchases of goods (for resale). Cash purchases go to the Cash Book; asset purchases to the Journal.
8.concept: Purchases Book: only credit purchases of goods.

9.exp: Debit is larger → Debit balance = 85,000 − 62,000 = ₹23,000. "By Balance c/d 23,000" is written on the Credit side to make both sides equal (85,000).

10.exp: The smaller side (Credit 25,000) is increased by 15,000 to 40,000; so "By Balance c/d" goes on the Credit side; in the next period "To Balance b/d" goes on the Debit side.
10.concept: Balance c/d on the smaller side; b/d on the opposite side.

11.exp: Closing = 18,200 + 7,300 − 9,650 = ₹15,850. C wrongly adds the payments too.

12.concept: Types of Cash Book: single / double / three column.

13.exp: A discount given to a customer = Discount Allowed (expense) → Debit side (Receipts side). Discount Received → Credit side.
13.concept: Discount Allowed = Dr side; Discount Received = Cr side.

14.exp: To bring the Imprest back to the original amount, reimburse exactly what was spent = ₹3,640. (₹1,360 is already in hand.)

15.exp: If a whole transaction is omitted, both Dr and Cr stay short → the TB still agrees. In A, C and D, Dr ≠ Cr and the error is found.
15.concept: A TB does not guarantee all errors are caught.

16.exp: Credit is short (2,38,000); so the difference of ₹7,000 is put on the Credit side in the Suspense A/c. Difference = 2,45,000 − 2,38,000.
16.concept: The difference goes to Suspense on the short side.

17.exp: Goods returned by a customer = Sales Return (Returns Inwards) → Sales Returns Book. The Purchases Returns Book is for goods we return to a supplier.
17.concept: Sales return = returned by the customer.

19.exp: Credit is short by 7,000 and Debit is excess by 7,000 → total difference ₹14,000 (double the amount).

21.exp: Anil A/c: Dr 18,000 (sales); Cr 10,000 (bank) → Debit balance ₹8,000 (receivable from him).

22.exp: Only credit purchases go in the Purchases Book: 12,000 + 8,500 + 5,750 = ₹26,250. The cash purchase goes in the Cash Book.

23.exp: Total expenses = 1,250+870+640+400 = 3,160. Balance = 5,000 − 3,160 = ₹1,840. The Head Cashier gives ₹3,160 to restore ₹5,000.

24.exp: In an Error of Principle (e.g. debiting Machinery for repairs) the amount is the same on both sides, so the TB agrees but the classification is wrong. In the other three, Dr ≠ Cr.
24.concept: An agreeing TB does not mean the accounts are error-free.

1.exp: A BRS explains why the two records show different balances (timing differences, errors).

2.exp: Issued by us but not yet reached the bank = Unpresented (issued but not presented). It reduced the Cash Book; the Passbook has not reduced yet.
2.concept: Unpresented cheque: Passbook balance is higher.

3.exp: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; the cost of the asset is spread over the years and shown as an expense.

4.exp: SLM: (Cost − Scrap value) ÷ life = the same amount every year. In WDV it decreases every year.

5.exp: Trading A/c has Sales, Purchases, Opening/Closing Stock, direct expenses → Gross Profit.

6.exp: Net Profit = Gross Profit + other incomes − indirect expenses. Purchases/Stock have already gone into the Trading A/c.

7.exp: Balance Sheet = as on a date (e.g. 31 March). P&L = for a period.
7.concept: Balance Sheet = a statement of position.

8.exp: An expense directly linked to purchasing goods = Direct expense → Trading A/c Debit.
8.concept: Direct expenses: Wages, Carriage Inwards, Freight.

9.exp: Unpresented cheques reduced the Cash Book but not the bank; so the Passbook is higher = 25,000 + 4,000 = ₹29,000.

10.concept: Adjust the Cash Book for items not yet recorded.

12.exp: Year 1: 5,000; Book value 45,000. Year 2: 45,000 × 10% = ₹4,500. 5,000 is the SLM answer.
12.concept: WDV = % on the previous Book Value.

13.concept: GP = Net Sales − Cost of Goods Sold.

14.exp: NP = 1,80,000 + 6,000 − (40,000 + 18,000) = ₹1,28,000. Commission received is income, so it is added.
14.concept: Net Profit = GP + incomes − indirect expenses.

15.exp: Expense for this year = paid + outstanding = 22,000 + 2,000 = ₹24,000. Outstanding Rent is a Liability in the Balance Sheet.

16.exp: 9,000 − 1,500 = ₹7,500. Prepaid Insurance is a Current Asset in the Balance Sheet.

17.exp: Creditors must be paid soon (within 1 year) → Current Liability. Debtors, Stock = Current Assets; Furniture = Fixed Asset.
17.concept: Current Liabilities = dues to be paid within 1 year.

19.exp: Annual dep = 12,000. After 2 years Book Value = 1,20,000 − 24,000 = ₹96,000.

20.exp: First adjust the Cash Book: 18,500 − 100 = 18,400. Then + unpresented 3,200 − uncollected deposit 5,000 = ₹16,600.
20.concept: BRS: every timing item in the right direction.

22.concept: In a Balance Sheet Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

23.concept: Net Profit ratio = NP ÷ Net Sales × 100.

24.exp: Sale price is below Book Value: loss = 60,000 − 52,000 = ₹8,000 (Loss on sale of asset).
24.concept: Profit/Loss on sale = Sale price − Book value.

2.exp: The Union Finance Minister chairs the GST Council; the State finance ministers are members.

3.exp: As per the 56th GST Council (3 Sep 2025) the two main rates are 5% (merit) and 18% (standard); 40% on selected sin/luxury goods. 12% and 28% were the earlier rates. As of 2026-10-19 — rates can change.
3.concept: GST rate structure (as of 22 Sep 2025 onward).

4.exp: CGST = Central GST → Central Government. SGST → State Government.

5.exp: Output GST = what we charge on sales; Input GST = what we pay on purchases.

6.exp: A unique 15-digit number given to a registered person (first 2 digits are the state code, then the PAN).

7.exp: The payer deducts tax at source and deposits it with the government; the payee gets credit for it.

8.exp: PAN = Permanent Account Number (10 characters) — Income Tax Department.

12.concept: Intra-state GST: the rate splits into two equal halves.

13.exp: GSTR-1 = outward supplies; GSTR-3B = summary return and tax payment. ITR is for Income Tax.

14.exp: ITC needs a valid tax invoice/documents, receipt of goods/services, tax paid by the supplier etc.; ITC is blocked on some expenses.

15.exp: 2,00,000 × 1% = ₹2,000. Rates/thresholds can change — as of 2026-10-19, based on a secondary source; verify on incometax.gov.in.

16.exp: TDS = 10,000; amount received = 1,00,000 − 10,000 = ₹90,000. (Rate: secondary source, as of 2026-10-19.)

17.exp: The new Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 (per many sources). 1 July 2017 was the start of GST.

19.exp: Inter-state → IGST: 80,000 × 18% = ₹14,400. 7,200 = 9% (one part of CGST/SGST) — wrong.

20.exp: Salary TDS: estimated annual tax ÷ 12 = 24,000 ÷ 12 = ₹2,000 per month.

21.exp: Exports are zero-rated; i.e. no tax on goods/services leaving the country and ITC on inputs can be refunded (as per rules).

22.exp: 3,00,000 × 40% = ₹1,20,000. (Selected goods: see the full list on PIB/CBIC.)

23.exp: The new Act uses one concept, "Tax Year" (e.g. Tax Year 2026-27). (Secondary sources; verify the official text.)

24.exp: ₹4–8 lakh: 4,00,000 × 5% = 20,000. ₹8–10 lakh: 2,00,000 × 10% = 20,000. Total = ₹40,000. (Actual tax differs because of rebate/cess/standard deduction.)

1.exp: The financial year in India is 1 April to 31 March; the Budget is for this period.

2.exp: Article 112 — Annual Financial Statement (laid before Parliament every year).

3.exp: An electricity bill is a regular (running) expense = Revenue Expenditure; the others create long-lasting assets = Capital.

4.exp: Borrowings and sale of assets (disinvestment) are Capital Receipts; taxes and interest are Revenue Receipts.
4.concept: Capital receipt = increases liabilities / reduces assets.

5.exp: Deficit = expenditure more, receipts less. The opposite is a Surplus Budget.

6.exp: Voucher = proof of payment/receipt (bill, receipt, authorisation). No payment without a voucher.

7.exp: If one person has all the powers there is a risk of misuse; so duties are separated.

8.exp: If expenses are lower it is favourable; if higher it is unfavourable (Adverse).

10.exp: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts = 12,00,000 − 9,50,000 = ₹2,50,000.

11.exp: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Receipts (excluding borrowings) = 53,47,315 − 36,51,547 = ₹16,95,768 crore. (4.3% of GDP per PRS.)
11.concept: Fiscal deficit = the government's total borrowing need.

12.exp: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest payments = 8,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.

13.exp: Money received by selling an asset/investment = Capital Receipt.

14.exp: Article 267 — Contingency Fund (for unforeseen expenditure, held at the President's disposal). Article 266 — Consolidated Fund.

15.exp: A daily reconciliation (cash count) catches mistakes and misappropriation early.

16.exp: In ZBB every activity's cost is justified again without relying on last year's figures.

17.exp: Budget = 2,85,000; Actual = 2,95,000 → ₹10,000 extra spent = Adverse. (Salaries 5,000 favourable; Travel 15,000 adverse; net 10,000 adverse.)
17.concept: Net variance = Σ Actual − Σ Budget.

18.exp: Unspent = 5,00,000 − 3,85,000 = ₹1,15,000. Unspent grant must be returned/adjusted as per rules.

19.exp: New AC + installation = 3,15,000 (Capital). Repair 80,000 = Revenue Expenditure.
19.concept: Cost of an asset = price + installation.

20.exp: Payment without a voucher/approval violates internal control; the expense can be disallowed in audit.

22.exp: Under Article 114 money cannot be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without an Appropriation Bill/Act.

1.exp: The RBI was established on 1 April 1935; nationalised in 1949.

2.exp: The central office of the RBI is in Mumbai.

3.exp: KYC = Know Your Customer (identity and address proof when opening a bank account).

4.exp: A Current Account suits frequent transactions (generally no interest). Savings is for personal savings.

5.exp: "Account Payee" crossing means the amount is not paid in cash; it is credited to the payee's account — safer.

6.exp: NEFT runs 24x7x365 and settles in half-hourly batches.

7.exp: RBI FAQ: "minimum ₹2,00,000 with no upper or maximum ceiling". RTGS is 24x7x365 (since 14 Dec 2020).

8.exp: Never share a PIN/OTP; the bank never asks for it.

9.exp: IFSC = 11 characters: first 4 letters identify the bank, the 5th is 0, the last 6 identify the branch. (9 = MICR; 15 = GSTIN.)

10.exp: A cheque is valid for 3 months from the date of issue; after that it is a "stale cheque".

11.exp: Repo rate = the rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks. (The current rate changes — see the RBI's Monetary Policy Statement for the exact figure.)
11.concept: Repo rate = RBI → banks lending rate.

12.exp: CRR = a fixed part of the bank's total deposits must be kept with the RBI; in SLR, however, gold/government securities/cash are kept with the bank itself.

13.exp: As per NPCI's IMPS information, ₹5 lakh per transaction (excluding SMS/IVR). A bank may set a lower limit.

14.exp: NEFT = in batches (every half hour); RTGS = each transaction individually in real time (gross).
14.concept: NEFT batch vs RTGS gross real-time.

15.exp: RD = a fixed amount every month; FD = a lump sum.

16.exp: Insufficient funds → dishonour. If conditions are met, action can follow under NI Act s.138 (notice, time limits apply).

17.exp: Interest for 1 year = 80,000 × 7.5% = 6,000; 6 months = half a year → ₹3,000. 6,000 = full year; 83,000 = principal + 6 months' interest.
17.concept: Interest for part of a year.

18.exp: Year 1: 10,000 × 1.10 = 11,000; Year 2: 11,000 × 1.10 = ₹12,100. With simple interest it would be 12,000. ₹2,100 is only the interest.

19.exp: Closing = 20,000 + 15,000 − 8,500 = ₹26,500. A Credit in the customer's account = money deposited.

20.exp: As per the RBI, RTGS has a minimum of ₹2,00,000; for 1,50,000 NEFT/IMPS/UPI can be used.

21.exp: No PIN is needed to receive money; entering the PIN sends money out. Reject the request and report to the bank/cyber helpline.

22.exp: Interest = 1,20,000 × 12% = 14,400; total = 1,34,400; instalment = 1,34,400 ÷ 12 = ₹11,200. (A real bank EMI differs because it uses the reducing balance.)

1.exp: CPU = Central Processing Unit — the "brain" of the computer.

2.exp: Output = gives information out from the computer (Monitor, Printer). Keyboard, Mouse, Scanner = Input devices.

3.exp: Ctrl+Z = Undo; Ctrl+Y = Redo; Ctrl+C = Copy; Ctrl+X = Cut.

6.exp: CC = Carbon Copy. BCC = Blind Carbon Copy (not visible to other recipients).

8.exp: Column is a letter (B) and Row is a number (5). B5 = Column B, Row 5.

14.exp: Files are stored online; they can be accessed and shared from anywhere (with proper permissions).

15.exp: A long, unique password with mixed characters is safe; not a simple/guessable one.

16.exp: Deleted files go to the Recycle Bin; they can be restored from there.
